body:
Do you need a college degree to become a real estate agent in Florida?

No. Florida does not require a college degree to become a licensed real estate agent. What the state requires instead is a high school diploma or GED, completion of a 63-hour pre-license course, passing the state licensing exam, and clearing a background check. Thousands of agents build successful careers in Florida without ever setting foot in a college classroom.

What Florida actually requires to get licensed

The Florida Department of Business and Professional Regulation (DBPR) sets a handful of core requirements for a sales associate license: you must be at least 18 years old, hold a high school diploma or its equivalent (a GED works fine), complete the state-approved 63-hour pre-license course, and pass the Florida real estate sales associate exam. A background check, including fingerprinting, is also part of the process. None of these steps involve a college transcript of any kind.

How long the licensing process typically takes

Without a degree requirement in the way, the timeline for getting licensed mostly comes down to how quickly you move through the course and exam process, not years spent in a classroom. The 63-hour pre-license course can be finished in as little as two to three weeks of steady, full-time study, or spread out over a couple of months around a job or family schedule, since most approved schools offer it self-paced online. After finishing the course, you schedule the state exam, and the background check and fingerprinting typically process within a few weeks. Many people move from enrolling in a course to holding an active Florida license in two to four months, without ever touching a college application or a four-year timeline.

The 63-hour pre-license course

This course is where the real preparation happens. It covers real estate law, contracts, finance, appraisal, and ethics, the practical knowledge you actually need on day one with a client. It’s offered by state-approved schools online or in person, and it’s built for people coming from any background, not just those with a business or finance degree. You’ll need to pass the course’s own final exam before you’re eligible to sit for the state test.

Passing the state licensing exam

After the pre-license course, you sit for the state exam, administered through a state-approved testing vendor. It covers real estate math, national principles and practices, and Florida-specific law and statutes. It’s a rigorous exam, but it’s testing what you learned in the pre-license course, not a college curriculum. Plenty of agents without a single college credit pass it on their first attempt with focused study.

Where a college degree actually helps (but isn’t required)

There is one place a degree matters, and it’s easy to confuse with a requirement: agents who hold a four-year degree in real estate from an accredited institution can be exempt from Florida’s separate 45-hour post-licensing course, the education required before your first license renewal. That’s a benefit for the small number of agents who happen to have that specific degree, not a barrier for everyone else. If you don’t have a real estate degree, you simply complete the 45-hour course like most new agents do, and your license stays on track either way.

What if you already have an unrelated college degree?

An unrelated degree, in business, education, hospitality, or anything else, doesn’t change your path at all. It doesn’t shorten the pre-license course, exempt you from the state exam, or waive the background check. The only degree that has any effect on the Florida licensing process is a real estate-specific four-year degree from an accredited school, and even then it only affects the later post-licensing step, not whether you can get your initial license in the first place. In practice, your major, or the fact that you never finished a degree at all, simply isn’t part of the equation the state looks at.

Why real estate rewards more than a diploma

Real estate success has less to do with formal education and more to do with people skills, follow-through, and local market knowledge. Agents come from backgrounds in retail, hospitality, teaching, the military, and dozens of other fields with no college degree at all. What separates agents who thrive from agents who struggle is usually work ethic, communication, and a willingness to learn the market, not a diploma on the wall. Brokerages that invest in real training and mentorship tend to matter far more to a new agent’s success than anything on a transcript.

Getting licensed is the easy part, choosing where to start is what matters

Once you clear these requirements and hold an active Florida license, the next decision, and often the more important one, is which brokerage you activate under. Adams, Cameron & Co., the area’s largest brokerage since 1963 in Daytona Beach, has helped new agents from every kind of background get real training and mentorship from day one, degree or no degree. Start a conversation about what getting licensed and launching your career here actually looks like.

Licensing requirements can change; confirm current details with the Florida DBPR before you begin. Educational only, not legal advice.

faq.q: Do you need any specific degree to become a real estate agent in Florida?
faq.a: No. Florida requires only a high school diploma or GED, not a college degree of any kind, to qualify for a real estate sales associate license.

faq.q: Does a real estate degree help at all if it's not required?
faq.a: Yes, in one specific way: a four-year real estate degree from an accredited institution can exempt you from Florida's 45-hour post-licensing course required before your first renewal. It doesn't change the initial licensing requirements.

faq.q: What education do you actually need to get licensed in Florida?
faq.a: You need a high school diploma or GED, completion of a state-approved 63-hour pre-license course, a passing score on the state exam, and a clean background check.

faq.q: Can someone with no college background succeed as a real estate agent?
faq.a: Yes. Many successful agents in Florida have no college degree at all. The job rewards relationship-building, follow-through, and local market knowledge more than formal education.
